articles.title: Donald Trump’s Korea Diplomacy Is a Distraction Exercise
articles.author: Kap Seol
articles.content: Donald Trump has made several recent overtures to North Korean leader Kim Jong-un for a new summit, seven years after their meeting in Hanoi ended inconclusively. Over the summer, he abruptly reduced the scale of the annual US–South Korea joint military exercises. Four times in the space of nine days, he posted pictures of Kim on his Truth Social account in an apparent wooing exercise. These efforts have so far failed to lure Kim to the negotiation table. Kim Yo-jong, his powerful sister who occupies the number-two position in the North Korean hierarchy, declared on August 19 that North Korea has no interest in a new summit with the United States. At the same time, she left a door slightly ajar by remarking that her brother retains good memories and feelings about Trump from their past summits. Trump responded in kind by sharing four throwback pictures of the two on Truth Social. South Korea’s spy agency, the National Intelligence Service, reported to lawmakers that a summit between Trump and Kim could take place at any time, citing signs of dialogue between Washington and Pyongyang. Kim, however, appears to be raising the ante from their last summit. He will not sit down with Trump again unless the latter takes denuclearization off the table and the United States and South Korea suspend all military drills ahead of a summit. Ultimately, North Korea is now seeking arms-control talks with the US and international recognition of its status as a nuclear power. A Useful Diversion It was Trump who gained the most from the 2019 Hanoi summit, as he could divert public and media attention toward Vietnam’s capital and away from Washington, where the congressional testimony of Michael Cohen, his former personal attorney, was underway. He is now apparently using North Korea as a distraction again, this time from his disastrous failure in Iran. For Kim, on the other hand, Hanoi was a nightmarish experience that could have threatened his monolithic control of the country. At the time, Kim was confident that he could reach a deal with Trump, allowing US inspections of North Korea’s known nuclear sites in return for a relaxation of economic sanctions. This would be a preliminary step toward a peace treaty to formally end the Korean War and normalize diplomatic ties. Before hopping on his luxurious train that would take more than sixty hours to reach Hanoi, Kim hosted a huge departure ceremony. Some high-ranking officials wept with joy in anticipation of the concessions they expected to gain from Washington and Seoul after seven decades of bone-crushing sanctions and forced isolation. Instead, the summit ended without an agreement, as Trump abruptly demanded access to additional sites for inspection. Kim had to ride the same luxurious, slow train back to Pyongyang, empty-handed and deeply humiliated. Later that year, Trump and Kim had an impromptu meeting at the joint security area of the demilitarized zone (DMZ) dividing North and South Korea, in a move widely seen as a face-saving gesture for Kim and another headline-grabbing public stunt for Trump. Following the Hanoi fiasco, in which it had unusually high political and economic stakes, the Kim regime appeared to show signs of distress. Kim and his sister responded strongly, ordering the explosive demolition of a liaison building built by South Korea at the joint security area and blaming the Hanoi failure on Seoul’s role as a supposedly clumsy and deceptive middleman. Kim also enacted a law that authorized the death penalty for watching or distributing South Korean movies and music, which had become a clandestine national pastime for his people. North Korea further accelerated the development and production of nuclear warheads without feeling the need to conduct another test, which underscored the maturity of its nuclear technology. It now has fifty-seven “very powerful” warheads, according to Trump, although South Korea puts the figure at 120. Kim also sought to appease the populace, which culminated in his public apology in 2020 for failing to do enough to improve their difficult livelihoods. He severed all dialogue and shredded existing agreements with Seoul, renouncing reunification as a national goal. Nevertheless, during Trump’s first term, Kim never stopped exchanging letters with the US president, urging him to engage in direct dialogue without South Korean meddling. The Grandson Also Rises Kim’s entrenchment finally began to pay off in October 2024 when he dispatched an estimated 12,000 to 15,000 special operations troops to fight against Ukraine for Russia. North Korea had already been selling artillery shells and missiles to Russia, which in return helped its ally to circumvent sanctions and provided it with hard currency, military technology, and flour. The benefits were starkly visible even on North Korean state television, which began broadcasting a series of “flour food” exhibitions in a country where rice is the staple food. As Kim sought to lean toward Russia, China has felt obliged to mend its relations with North Korea, which had previously deteriorated after Beijing began complying with the international sanctions regime. China steadily increased trade with North Korea to keep Pyongyang at arm’s length from Moscow. This trade rose 22 percent year over year during the first two months of 2026, after recovering to its pre-pandemic level in 2025. North Korea’s economic and political rebound coincides with the decline of the US-dominated unipolar order. To Pyongyang, this decline means the restoration of an old bipolar order, under which North Korea stands to benefit from the military rivalry between the United States and its allies on the one hand and China and Russia on the other. Just as was the case during the Cold War era, Pyongyang can play the competing powers off against each other as they vie for influence over a strategically located and politically important region. It should thus come as little surprise that Pyongyang is now enjoying a niche economic boom, strong enough to draw attention from such business media outlets as The Wall Street Journal , the Financial Times , and Bloomberg . The upturn appears to be real, making Gucci bags and Ikea furniture affordable to Pyongyang’s elite and keeping the lights on at ports and heavy industry plants along the east coast. However, the rising North Korean tide still appears to be too low to lift all ships, at least for now. Most of all, the cost is being paid in the blood of working-class children shed on foreign soil. About 2,300 North Korean soldiers were killed during their first deployments alongside Russian forces, according to the BBC. In August 2025, Kim cried publicly again at the opening ceremony of a memorial for those killed in combat. On the Eve of Something If the Trump–Kim summit does go ahead, it will unfold against a highly complex global backdrop. Iran and the United Stats are still at war. Iran supplies drones to Russia; North Korea supplies combat personnel, artillery shells, and missiles to Russia; South Korea provides ammunition and artillery shells to Ukraine through Poland and the US; China supplies drone components to Iran and Russia, and food and other resources to North Korea; Russia supplies military technology, food, and financial support to North Korea; and Ukrainian drones recently sank an Iranian freight ship in the Caspian Sea. Many South Koreans are concerned that a new Trump–Kim summit could heighten tensions on the peninsula rather than ease them as Trump’s overtures proceed while sidelining the South. The concerns are turning into anxiety, as starkly reflected in a recent Gallup Korea poll conducted after the truncated military drill. About two-thirds of respondents said that South Korea should have its own nuclear weapons, while only 30 percent were opposed to such a move. South Korea is playing catch-up in response to Trump’s overtures and the replies from Kim, with all communication between Seoul and Pyongyang severed and a small White House coterie pursuing behind-the-scenes diplomacy. Although South Korea’s liberal president, Lee Jae-myong, welcomed Trump’s unilateral move, he also said he would accelerate efforts to regain wartime operational control of the South Korean military from the US — a form of control that Washington arrogated to itself during the Korean War back in 1950. It has been promising to relinquish this authority since 1989 but has yet to do so. After North Korea amended its constitution in May 2026 to define the two Koreas as two hostile states rather than parts of a divided nation, much of South Korea’s nationalist left found itself in disarray. Supporters of this political tendency had long regarded North Korea as the more independent and self-reliant of the two, viewing the South as a prosperous US lackey destined to follow the North’s lead in the process of reunification. Any US deal with North Korea that does not involve South Korea will likely prompt Seoul to go nuclear on its own or seek some form of nuclear deterrence. Jeong Se-hyun is a former reunification minister and an architect of the engagement policy with the North under the liberal government of Nobel Peace Laureate Kim Dae-jung. In a recent radio interview , he said that South Korea should demand that the United States redeploy to the South tactical nuclear warheads that it withdrew in 1991 if Washington recognizes the North as a nuclear power. The world’s tenth-largest arms exporter is also now in the final stage of launching a nuclear-powered submarine. Summitry A deal that ultimately excludes the South is unlikely, given that Trump will probably expect Seoul (in combination with Japan) to foot the bill for any agreement with Pyongyang. However, tensions and mistrust will continue to linger. After all, we are seeing an attempt at a historic initiative by an octogenarian, autocratic figure with a severely limited attention span, who is dealing with a young and shrewd dictator willing to retain the power he inherited from his grandfather through his father, at the expense of the lives of his own young soldiers. Nevertheless, in a world increasingly engulfed by wars and conflicts on a global scale, even a summit like this would be better than no rapprochement at all between the state with the world’s largest nuclear arsenal and a de facto nuclear power. No one should mistake it for peace, even if Kim cries in public again. The Left should be watching this space closely and cautiously for potential openings to build a strong antinuclear peace campaign from below.

articles.title: An Agenda for De-Alienating Work
articles.author: Peter Dorman
articles.content: Wages have been bad for years, but the quality of work hasn’t fared much better. Gig work, with its insecurity and minimal protection from managerial whims, has proliferated. New technology has enabled a degree of workforce surveillance that previous generations would have regarded as unacceptable. The degradation of corporate work at all levels is an important aspect of enshittification . Unsurprisingly, you can now click across multiple websites advising you how to look like you’re doing your job when your brain is somewhere else. And now AI is poised to usher us — those who still have jobs — into a new era of management-by-slop. Where can we look for an agenda to fight back? There’s a branch of left-wing thought that focuses on exactly these kinds of problems: the theory of alienation. Karl Marx argued that capitalism alienates workers from the products of their labor, from control over their work activity and their capacity to develop themselves through it, and by separating them from the communal life of their coworkers, making them competitors instead of comrades. After capitalism is swept away by the working class, such alienation will presumably disappear. Unfortunately, this theory makes sweeping claims without providing much practical guidance for identifying the problem in real-world contexts, understanding its causes, and taking steps to counteract it. I think it’s better to start over, using more familiar social science concepts and beginning with the important distinction between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation. Extrinsic motivation is the system of rewards and punishments that push you toward the choices and actions someone else wants you to take. Getting paid to do a job is the most obvious example. Intrinsic motivation comes from the purpose or experience of the action itself. Recreational sports and cooking a dinner for your household are things you do for their own value, not, usually, for extrinsic reasons. Beyond Feeding the Face Before going any further, two clarifications are in order. First, these two kinds of motivation are not mutually exclusive. Things we do for money often have an intrinsic pull as well — in fact, they should, and their combined effect can be reinforcing. Second, this distinction implies no priority or relative importance, no hierarchy of needs as in the work of Abraham Maslow , nor an injunction, as Bertolt Brecht so elegantly put it , to “first feed the face.” Each of us values the different aspects of work in our own way, and the purpose of this short discussion is to get a lay of the land, not to elevate one personal philosophy over others. Of course, most jobs are undertaken, initially at least, mainly for extrinsic reasons, and the extrinsic benefits we want them to offer are fairly obvious and uncontroversial. A quick list should do: a good job provides ample pay and benefits. It offers a predictable schedule and the workload the worker is looking for. It comes with enough job security to reduce stress and make it easier to plan ahead. It doesn’t expose the worker to undue risk of injury or disease. It provides opportunities to learn skills and move up, with prospects for better future benefits. Realistically, any economic system has to provide enough of these things to draw workers to the work that needs doing, and a good system will go beyond this minimum. It’s when we get to the intrinsic attributes that more nuance is needed. A natural entry point is to distinguish between the work itself and the workplace. For the first, I think there are two dimensions, the nature of the work and how purposeful it is. Good work of the first sort is mentally and/or physically satisfying. It hones expertise and craft, making us some combination of smarter, stronger, and more confident in our abilities. An essential aspect of this is variety, doing many different things rather than the same thing over and over. Often the most important step is to break up an overly rigid division of labor, so skill isn’t smothered by routine. Purposefulness is more complicated. There are actually two requirements for meaningful work, neither sufficient without the other. First, workers have to recognize the connection between their own input and the ultimate product. If work is highly subdivided, or if parts of it are assigned to different teams working in isolation from each other, this connection may be lost. Recognition of this issue has led to sporadic managerial interest in more integrative forms of work organization. But the second requirement is also essential: workers have to feel that the end product is genuinely valuable and lends meaning to the work they’re doing. Of course, what counts as a meaningful outcome depends on how well the values of workers are reflected in what they produce. This is subjective, but not entirely. If a firm exploits its customers or suppliers, its workforce is less likely to take pride in their role. Think about customer service call centers. Some really do offer the sort of help they advertise, while others just go through the motions. Surely the workers wearing the headsets know the difference, and the satisfaction they might derive from their hours spent on the phone will reflect this. My underlying point is that, in this respect, meaningful work depends on whether the business has a purpose beyond just making money. The Common Life of Work This leaves the other source of intrinsic benefit, derived less from the work than the workplace in which it occurs. Much of this is simply the joy of social connection: making friends and being part of a team. How much of this a given job offers is contingent. Sometimes the chemistry is there and sometimes it isn’t. But jobs can be organized to provide more opportunities to socialize, from the layout of the work environment to the structure of the workflow. (Policies on working from home often reduce some kinds of social connection while increasing others.) But being part of a community is about much more than friendly chatter. The workplace is a realm of life in common. It establishes rules and expectations for what its members should do, distributing the gains and burdens of collaboration. It is organized hierarchically, and for all these reasons it is thoroughly political. If workers think the workplace is run fairly, giving them the voice they deserve, they will benefit both by getting better treatment on the job and from the process that makes it happen. (This combines what social scientists call “outcome” and “process” benefits.) Not surprisingly, then, self-management is a key element in the intrinsic value of work, but discussion of it tends to be overgeneralized. Let’s unpack the idea, based on the recognition that what we are really talking about is self-government in a workplace setting. Using the template of politics, I suggest three dimensions, each somewhat independent of the others. Let’s call them freedom, participation, and representation. Freedom, Participation, and Representation Freedom : in a work context, this means minimizing supervision and the imposition of hierarchical authority — in a word, autonomy. Autonomy may be individual if a single worker is allowed to do their work in their own way, out of management purview, and is responsible only for delivering a product at the end of the process. University professors, especially if tenured, have a lot of autonomy in this sense, which is why these jobs are sought after despite usually paying less than alternatives requiring similar credentials. But autonomy can also apply to a team, and many workplaces are organized on the basis of autonomous team production. All else being equal, reliance on co-responsibility rather than intrusive management gives workers more freedom to control their work, although the difference may be trivial if the production goals feel excessive or pointless. Participation : We often speak of management as a group of people, and certainly some employees are classified as managers and others not. But management can also be understood as a set of decisions that need to be made at each level of the organization, often routinely. Those decisions can be shared, depending on the skills of the workforce, the way the work process has been organized, and the willingness of those in authority to collaborate with those beneath them on the organizational charts. Management theorists like W. Edwards Deming and Stafford Beer tried to convince the top echelons that shared decision-making was not only humane and respectful, but would also benefit the bottom line. Cross-training workers and giving them opportunities to learn management skills, they both thought, would allow the firm to devolve more responsibility on them. Beer in particular stressed horizontal communication between work units, so they could coordinate without having to involve, and be subjected to, higher-ups. Representation : Most of the theorizing and advocacy in the realm of self-management has been about systems in which workers select representatives who bring their voice to firm-level decision-making. This is what unions do when they bargain collectively, and it is also a function performed by works councils and laws, as in Germany , that require worker representatives to serve on company boards of directors. It is at the core of the democratic justification for worker cooperatives, since each worker gets one vote on key questions of policy and leadership. The argument for representative democracy is broadly the same at the workplace as it is in society at large, although there are important differences based on who is a “citizen” of the workplace polity and what other groups of “citizens” ought to have a voice in those decisions as well. That is, enterprises are far more entangled with other enterprises and the communities they operate in than governments are with other governments — although there is a case to be made that national sovereignty is also too great in an interdependent world. I’ve spent time on the workplace governance aspect of intrinsic motivation because enthusiasts for one dimension or another tend to subsume the entire question under their chosen focus. Worker autonomy, participation in decision-making, and representation in organization-wide issues are all valuable, but none of them ensures the others. Each in its own way points to attributes of a freer and fairer economic system than the one we currently inhabit. Work and Alienation So now let us return to Marx and his theory of alienation, since there are important lessons to be learned for the quality of work in capitalism and beyond. I take them to be these: The schema here is similar to Marx’s but differs in important ways. For Marx, workers are alienated because they lose control over the things they produce; on the account offered here, there is little meaning in work if the end product isn’t seen as valuable. The problem with Marx’s version is that workers always cede control over their work products: they create them for others to take and use. Even an artist doesn’t expect to have final say over a painting once a buyer, like a museum, takes possession. And that can lead to frustration at times! But that’s how it has to be. The meaning a worker gets from producing something, on the other hand, usually survives its sale if it’s there to begin with. Another of Marx’s forms of alienation involves estrangement from one’s innate physical and mental capacities to create, and is virtually identical to the absence of the intrinsic benefit work should offer in employing and developing our creative potential. The difference is that, unlike Marx, this model doesn’t postulate that work has to be this way under capitalism or that abolishing capitalism is guaranteed to fix it. The third type of alienation, from the community of coworkers, presents a greater point of disagreement, however. Social stimulation doesn’t rise or fall with changes in the mode of production, although it can be spurred by encouraging more interaction at work. The claim that labor markets, in themselves, pit workers against each other, strikes me as overdrawn (despite the nightmare vision of Donald Westlake’s The Ax ). Meanwhile, Marx offers no analysis of the workplace as a system of governance, simply assuming it is pure autocracy under capitalist ownership. I realize that Marx was a pioneer in this field, and it’s predictable that our understanding would improve over almost two centuries of further experience. However much his work should remain a vital starting point, it need not be the final word on the problems of work we face today. It’s important to recognize that workers are not just on the receiving end of job quality. They bring themselves to the job, and what that entails — the degree of care and interest they exercise, how much they push back against unnecessary or exploitive rules and expectations — makes a big difference in what ensues. That said, good work invites engagement, and the bad kind makes it seem futile. Think of workers in meat processing plants who make the same cut, over and over, as carcasses glide by, one slice or more per second . We can acknowledge worker agency while calling out the jobs that simply crush it. As the preceding discussion should make clear, sweeping terms like alienation can do a disservice if they give the impression that bad jobs are bad across the board and vice versa. Empirically, we find all sorts of combinations of good and bad attributes, although, for most of us, the bad are more frequent and frustrating. An interesting question is whether there is a correlation between good extrinsic and bad intrinsic features. This was the claim of libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick , who thought that if a job were more alienating it would pay higher wages in the labor market: competition would force employers to compensate workers monetarily for especially unpleasant or meaningless tasks. This parallels a similar claim about dangerous working conditions, which I have disputed elsewhere . Nozick’s argument is flawed but not dumb, and there are some jobs that work that way, although it’s not the norm. At the same time, a softer version of his point is worth considering: there are unavoidable trade-offs between the different things we look for on the job. For instance, how much a firm, even one owned by its workers, can afford to pay in wages is constrained by productivity and consumer demand, and both can sometimes conflict with measures that make work more pleasant and personally rewarding. Marx’s formulation implies that alienation at work is our fate as long as capitalism prevails, while doing away with that system guarantees us an unalienated future. Both are up for debate. Enormous improvement is possible right now if we understand the changes we need to make and can organize to fight for them. The European Union’s directive on European Works Councils is a stronger example, although it could be stronger still . If it falls short of our vision for worker self-management, it at least advances one piece of it. Meanwhile, the question of just what should replace capitalism is a bit easier to answer if we are clear on the criteria for how work should be organized. Simply asserting that a general condition of alienation settles in when capitalism takes over and is lifted when capitalism departs is not helpful. Yes, the potential for de-alienating work is greater if we replace private with social ownership, but it’s not zero under capitalism, nor unlimited in an idealized socialist future. To go deeper into how work can be made more rewarding, we would have to look closely at specific workplaces. For instance, what would it take for work at Amazon warehouses to become good, both extrinsically and intrinsically? Or in phone support centers, where workers guide users through the complexities of computer hardware and software? Or in fields and orchards, where crops are planted and harvested? Or at airports, or on road maintenance crews? Abstract theories need to connect with detailed knowledge based on firsthand experience. Rather than fulminating at alienation in a general way, what we need are broad-based movements to make work a lot better, incrementally now and systematically in the future.

articles.title: Jean-Luc Mélenchon Thinks He Has a Path to Victory
articles.author: Olly Haynes
articles.content: High above the waters of the Lac d’Aiguille in southeastern France, hundreds of drones formed the face of Maximilien Robespierre, the Jacobin deputy to the National Convention during the French Revolution. Then they shifted into a new form, as the face of Louise Michel, a key figure in the Paris Commune of 1871. The drones then split up again, only to regroup as the face of Thomas Sankara, the revolutionary leader of Burkina Faso. The music playing from the lakeside speakers sped up, and two drones dropped a banner, onto which was projected video from an accelerating series of rallies and speeches by France Insoumise (FI) and its presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Finally, as the thumping orchestral music, intercut with segments of the Marseillaise and the Internationale , reached its crescendo, the drones formed the French flag and the words “Victory in 2027” before scattering into the darkness. The show illustrated what the ten thousand people gathered in Valence for France Insoumise’s summer university, known as Amfis, hoped to achieve: winning the 2027 election, conquering state power, and adding their movement to a historical canon alongside past revolutionaries and communards. Taking place over four days from August 20–23, eight months out from the presidential election, this year’s Amfis was the largest it has ever been. Activists came from all over France to participate in talks ranging from sociological analyses of new arrivals in the French countryside, to interviews with the drag queens from the hit French iteration of Drag Race. Eclecticism aside, the discussion honed in on two main questions: how to win the presidential election, and how to navigate state power if it does achieves this. Navigating Power The question of how to navigate state power was discussed largely through historical reference points. They ranged from the failure of France’s 1980s Socialist President François Mitterrand to the 1973 coup against Chile’s Salvador Allende, Gabriel Boric’s more recent experience as president in that same country, and a recurring fixation on Syriza and the Greek debt crisis of the last decade. Stathis Kouvelakis, a former member of Syriza’s central committee and a teacher in France Insoumise’s cadre-training program at the Institut La Boétie, warned that a confrontation of some kind with the European Union would be inevitable. He reasoned that while France’s economic and political situation is better than Greece’s was, that crisis had also given Syriza cards to play that France Insoumise would probably not have at their disposal. He cited as an example Syriza’s ability to command well over majority support for a conflict with the Troika of international institutions. France Insoumise may never have this, even if it wins a presidential election. FI lawmaker Clémence Guetté, while briefing press on the networks France Insoumise is consulting within the civil service, raised the prospect of disobeying the EU treaties if they got in the way of implementing France Insoumise’s program. Meanwhile, the party’s coordinator Manuel Bompard agreed with the banker Matthieu Pigasse that part of France’s public debt could be canceled — a position Mélenchon reiterated the day after the festival, igniting a weeklong polemic. I got the sense that part of the goal of this year’s festival was preparing the activists, and by extension the press and the French public, for a conflict at the EU level should France Insoumise take office. Nonvoters, Future Voters To make these more than hypothetical discussions, first had to come the strategy for taking power. In a talk to a tent overflowing with people, alongside the sociologists Manuel Cervera-Marzal and Safia Dahani, it was Bompard who laid out France Insoumise’s path to power. To summarize: various studies have demonstrated that there is now an abstention gap in French politics between bourgeois and working-class neighborhoods. Better-off citizens go to the polls, while working-class citizens increasingly don’t. “This,” Bompard stressed, “was not always the case.” “During the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s, the poor voted in greater numbers than the rich. They did so because they believed that an alternative [communism] existed to the current society, the society responsible for the situation they were in. They believed in it. They thought it was possible, so they wanted to turn toward it.” This currently nonvoting part of the French population — in France Insoumise argot, “the fourth bloc” alongside the Left, the Macronites, and the far right — is key to Mélenchon’s strategy for beating his previous scores and reaching the runoff in 2027. Nonvoters in general are members of the social groups otherwise most likely to vote France Insoumise, such as young people. By current polling, they back France Insoumise at a rate of 48 percent in the eighteen-to-twenty-five-year-old age bracket and 33 percent in the twenty-six-to-thirty-year-old bracket. This, argued Bompard, gives the Mélenchon campaign a “massive growth opportunity,” allowing it to reach the second round. Speaking to Jacobin , France Insoumise lawmaker Jérôme Legavre argued that this has to be done by creating a “mass campaign. . . . that is, a campaign that’s aimed toward the mass of the population, particularly those who hate politics and political parties because they have been lied to, betrayed, scorned, and spat upon.” France Insoumise often insists that its program, L’Avenir en commun (“The Future in Common”) is the basis of the party, rather than personality or PR alone. It is a wide-ranging document, touching on issues ranging from nationalization of steel to satellite sovereignty, child protection measures, and how humanity should share the seas. Campaigning on this program does not mean overloading the voters with an unending policy blitz. In the first round, it means campaigning on specific issues that activate its likely electorate, like raising the minimum wage and introducing price controls on basic goods, taking a strong stance against the genocide in Palestine and pegging climate policies to weather events like heat waves that demonstrate the immediate reality of climate breakdown. According to Legavre, the first thing the party will have to do is hold mass public meetings like Amfis, which — he concedes — “speak largely to the already convinced,” but which leave people “amped up with energy that is essential for waging the campaign.” From there, the activists will go out across France’s territory, going door-to-door to convince people not just to vote Mélenchon but even just to sign up to the electoral register. This is a major subject for France Insoumise, Legavre told me. After all, “millions of people in France aren’t registered to vote, and when polling day comes, they go ‘oh shit, I’m not registered,’ but, by that point, it’s too late.” France Insoumise’s Caravanes Populaires initiative has already signed up 1,500 people to the electoral roll across the twelve days that it has been active. The party will “engage across all means of communication” including requesting help from artists and influencers to get people signed up. Legavre, a committed Trotskyist who emphasized his view that France maintains a colonial relationship to its overseas territories, also argued that a reserve of extra voters could come from such populations outside of mainland France. He told Jacobin about its Pacific Islander populations: “France Insoumise considers New Caledonia to be a colony, we have privileged relations with the FLNKS [Front de libération nationale kanak et socialiste, the islands’ pro-independence coalition], its activists and leaders. We have campaigned for the liberation of Christian Tein, the imprisoned president of the FLNKS. When [France Insoumise lawmakers] Mathilde Panot and Bastien Lachaud went to New Caledonia they were able to hold public meetings in areas and regions where no other politician from metropolitan France would be able to go. “The position we have taken, the fact that we immediately demanded Tein’s liberation, that Mélenchon declared he was a supporter of New Caledonian independence and that the first thing he would do if elected is declare independence for New Caledonia, is part of what helps us. I don’t know what turnout will be like because it remains a colony, but it’s evident that we are in a position that no other party can occupy.” Divided Left As well as abstentionists and votes from France’s colonial possessions, France Insoumise hopes to avoid the splits on the Left that occurred in 2022, when the Parti Communiste Français (PCF) leader Fabien Roussel stayed in the race, getting 2 percent of the vote — more than the margin that Mélenchon needed to reach the second round. In that same election, the Écologistes’ candidate, the centrist Yannick Jadot, also maintained his hopeless presidential bid, achieving 4 percent of the vote. While Roussel is again preparing his candidacy, today’s Écologistes leader Marine Tondelier — who is relatively more left-wing than her predecessor — is caught between two factions. One faction wants the party not to field a candidate and back the liberal Raphaël Glucksmann, whereas the other wants to back Mélenchon. Tondelier will submit the decision to run a candidate or not to a vote of Écologistes activists that will take place this autumn. France Insoumise aims to win the argument within the Écologistes, or at least prepare the ground for a swift withdrawal of their candidate should members decide they need Tondelier in the race. Cyrille Chatelain, an Écologistes lawmaker supportive of negotiations with France Insoumise was on two panels at the festival, and Mélenchon made sure to be photographed alongside her. Verts Populaires, a splinter group of Écologistes who backed France Insoumise in this spring’s local elections against their own party line, were also given a prominent display in the lakeside “village of associations.” France Insoumise lawmaker Guetté told journalists that there remains some room for programmatic negotiation with the Écologistes and PCF, but that they would prefer discussions to be extensive and not forged under pressure like the broad-left agreements reached for the 2022 and 2024 parliamentary elections. The hope on France Insoumise’s part is that a generous offer for a united list for the parliamentary elections that follow the 2027 presidential contest can secure Mélenchon as the only radical-left presidential candidate, either through the other parties not running, or through early withdrawals and endorsements. This was also part of the rationale for beginning his campaign early. As Francis Parny put it in his address to the general assembly of Insoumis Communistes (France Insoumise activists who are committed to communist ideas, many of them PCF members), every other party left of center is still focused internally, deciding who to support, or on how to run their primaries, while Mélenchon is talking to France about policy. Given this situation, and the fact that he is already polling above 15 percent, his supporters hope he can become the tactical vote on the Left with minimal fuss, and beat the centrist-neoliberal candidates to reach the second round. Bompard stressed in his talk that in the French presidential election there are two campaigns, adapted to the conditions of each round. France Insoumise’s gamble is that if Mélenchon reaches the second round a “launch window” will open up, in the words of Jérôme Legavre. They suggest that French politics will be entirely scrambled, polarized between those who fear the far right more, and thus back Mélenchon, and those who fear the left-winger and his program. Runoff While current polls show Mélenchon facing annihilation in the second round against Marine Le Pen (even the closest scenarios have him short of 40 percent), the abstention rates contained in those assumptions are unrealistic. Closer to such a runoff, it is likely that some of the abstainers would make up their mind in Mélenchon’s favor, narrowing the gap. Assuming France Insoumise’s calculations are correct and they can reach the second round, there remains a question mark over whether it can rely on the antifascist republican front that has blocked the far right from power since World War II. The framework of demonization has moved from Le Pen’s Rassemblement National to France Insoumise, today considered the main enemy of the Republic by most of the political and business elite. Both the center and the far right are currently deploying the same attack line, claiming to be best-placed to avoid the “chaos” of a France Insoumise government. In this connection, there is also something of a paradox in some of the analysis advanced by some supporters of Mélenchon’s candidacy. In his discussion with Bompard, sociologist Cervera-Marzal invoked the idea of “Macrono-Lepenism,” holding that there is an increasing convergence between the bloc around President Emmanuel Macron and Le Pen’s far right. If this is true — and there are plenty of examples to illustrate the concept — then relying on Macron’s rightward-moving voters to do their republican duty is surely a big roll of the dice. When I put this to Legavre, he was unfazed. What is occurring, in his view, is not a “fascistization of the French mind” but “a fascistization of the French elite.” Unfortunately for France Insoumise, what is required for them to make it through the first round is visibility, radicalism, and noise, but in the runoff they’ll need to be at least minimally reassuring to centrist voters, if these latter are to prefer Mélenchon to Le Pen. In the second round France Insoumise intends to address its campaign to the mass of the people, campaigning on issues where the Left enjoys majority support among the populace, and where the Right does not, such as repealing Macron’s pension reform, a version of which Le Pen now supports. Whether this will be enough to convince citizens to vote positively for Mélenchon, or at least to vote negatively against Le Pen, remains to be seen. In the evenings, when alcohol was permitted, the mood at the Amfis festival switched from one of dogged preparation and intellectual debate, to one of celebration and frivolity, with the political discussion switched out for DJ sets. Amfis is primarily an event for and by activists rather than for the mass public, and the crowds left with a renewed feeling of political possibility. Several activists speaking to me said that although they understood the scale of the challenge ahead, the festival had left them feeling like they could do it. I got the sense that whatever happens over the coming eight months, France Insoumise and their hundreds of thousands of activists are prepared to give it their all. They’ll be campaigning like their lives depend on it.

articles.title: Gloria Steinem Was the Godmother of Neoliberal Feminism
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Gloria Steinem, the establishment’s favorite radical feminist, died on September 2. The mainstream media has gone all out in praising her, with the Wall Street Journal and The New York Times united in their adulation. The Times called her the “personification of the women’s movement” and credited her with helping to usher in “sweeping cultural transformations across virtually every facet of American life, from the boardroom to the courtroom to the bedroom.” They approvingly quote her self-description as an “entrepreneur of social change.” For many people, she is the only radical feminist they can name, eclipsing the extraordinary women who planned and launched the successful women’s liberation movement starting in 1967. Steinem did wield enormous influence. Ms . magazine and the Ms. Foundation for Women, which she cofounded, came to define what was worthy in the feminist project. But to the women’s liberation pioneers she displaced, this meant silencing the radicals and promoting the anodyne. When Steinem described Ms . as “a kind of connective tissue for women all across this country who felt isolated until we came along and let them know they were not alone,” feminist pioneers saw Steinem as taking credit for work already done by the movement. The women’s liberation movement didn’t need Ms . to publicize it. It had already been on the front page of nearly every mass circulation magazine and had produced ten mass-market anthologies by 1971, selling millions of copies. The movement published one hundred small newspapers and journals, including Off Our Backs , It Ain’t Me Babe , and Woman’s World . And it had already won substantial victories by the time Steinem emerged on the scene. Thousands of working-class women were suing employers for sex discrimination. Abortion was legalized in New York State in 1970. The Equal Rights Amendment passed the House of Representatives in 1971 and the Senate in March 1972, followed immediately by twenty-two states. The Rise of Ms. Magazine So it was with an eye to the market already created by the radicals that Steinem, then thirty-seven and a professional magazine writer, collaborated with New York magazine editor Clay Felker to start Ms . magazine. The inaugural issue appeared as a section of New York in December 1971; it launched separately in July 1972. Washington Post publisher Katharine Graham invested, and Warner Communications put in $1 million but asked only for a 25 percent stake, an unusually generous arrangement. Some women’s liberation pioneers were at first glad to hear of the new publication. Kathie Sarachild of Redstockings , who coined the phrase “Sisterhood Is Powerful” and authored the germinal 1968 “Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising,” said she initially though Ms . would act as a feminist muckraker magazine, doing investigative journalism on behalf of women’s cause. She and other women’s liberation movement founders were soon disillusioned. It’s not that Steinem didn’t know who had led the movement up to the point she entered. In 1969, writing for New York magazine, she had attended the first-ever Redstockings abortion speak-out. She recalled the scene in her 1983 book, Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions : A local feminist group had asked women to testify about their real life experiences with illegal abortion. I sat in a church basement listening to women stand before an audience and talk about desperately trying to find someone who would help them, enduring pre-abortion rapes from doctors, being asked to accept sterilization as the price of abortion, and endangering their lives in an illegal, unsafe medical underground. . . . Suddenly I was no longer learning intellectually what was wrong. I knew. I had had an abortion when I was newly out of college, and had told no one. Yet the women who had taught her so much largely failed to find a place in the pages of Ms . three years later. Ellen Willis, pop music critic for The New Yorker and a Redstockings founder, did manage to make the cut starting in 1973. She resigned after two years, calling Ms . editorial policy “conservative, anti-left feminism.” In her resignation letter, Willis wrote: “No attempt has ever been made to recruit and hire experienced feminist writers, theorists, organizers. . . . Ms .’s politics [include] a mushy, sentimental idea of sisterhood designed to obscure political conflicts between women.” “Basically, it’s a change yourself line, the women’s magazine line,” Sarachild reflected later. “But the tricky thing about Ms . is that they pretend to be different. I bet there are certain women who wouldn’t bother reading women’s magazines who read Ms .” The editing reflected the politics, and radicals described Ms . editing as torture. Patricia Mainardi, author of the groundbreaking 1968 manifesto the “The Politics of Housework,” recalled: They would use a bullshit word instead of a strong word. I had the word “loved.” They changed it to “had a fondness for.” . . . Cindy Nemser wrote in an article about Alice Neel, “Alice Neel is the foremost portrait painter in our time.” In Ms . this became, “She may indeed be the foremost portrait painter of the last 40 years.” It’s sneaky editing, downgrading women’s contribution to art. Ms .’s line is women are no good in art. They have been oppressed and damaged by their oppression. They’re inferior. It’s a goody-goody line: we have to work harder to overcome our oppression. This made a sad contrast to the radicals, whose daring truth-telling had organized millions on the idea that what appeared to be women’s individual, personal problems were in fact political and rooted in their oppression by men. This was what they meant by the slogan “ The Personal Is Political .” Establishment Feminism Ms . pioneered the use of private foundation funding to steer feminist movement priorities. The Ms. Foundation dispensed money to approved feminist projects and created a database of feminists around the country and the world. It seeded the founding of the National Black Feminist Organization (NBFO), a Ms .-aligned black women’s group. The NBFO is often cited as the very first black feminist organization in the United States. Repeating the pattern for the women’s liberation movement as a whole, the group blotted out the more radical organizing that preceded it, including the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee Black Women’s Liberation Committee, its successor, the Third World Women’s Alliance, and the Patricia Robinson–led group Poor Black Women, all groups with radical and anti-imperialist politics. Before the rise of Ms ., movement originators had received widespread coverage. Kate Millett was on the cover of Time in 1970. That same year hundreds of feminists occupied the offices of Ladies’ Home Journal editor John Mack Carter, demanding an issue they edited (and free daycare for the magazine’s workforce). They won an eight-page supplement titled “The New Feminism.” But soon, the media went to Steinem for their “radical” feminism. Redstockings called it the “historic invisibility treatment”: The women who developed the movement’s strategy were written out of the picture. They became anonymous foremothers — while many were still in their twenties and thirties. Betty Friedan was too well-known to sideline, but the media loved to counterpose Steinem to Friedan, the older, unhip, allegedly less radical feminist who founded the National Organization for Women in 1966. In fact, Friedan’s politics were well to the left of Steinem’s — under her maiden name, Goldstein, Friedan had served as a staffer of the United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers of America, the union that held out against the demand that US unions expel their leftist leaders. While Friedan presented herself as reformist to evade red-baiting, she argued astutely for undermining the the basis of men’s power over women by advocating for programs and structures that would give women the economic foundation for independence from men. “Without childcare, it’s all just talk,” she argued. Steinem, styled as more radical, volunteered for Angela Davis’s bail committee, posed with her fist raised with Dorothy Pittman Hughes in October 1971, and toured the country with radical black lawyer Florynce Kennedy to lecture on feminism. Steinem loved witty aphorisms that expressed terrible politics. She quoted actress Lee Grant: “I’ve been married to a Marxist and a Fascist, and neither one of them ever took out the garbage.” Aside from garbage being a rare bit of male-coded housework, the quote implies that communists and fascists are equally bad. You wouldn’t expect a fascist to do housework. She liked to quote a woman cab driver in Boston who told her, “If men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament.” While funny, this gets the causality of women’s oppression backward. Founding radical feminist theorist Simone de Beauvoir argued that women are oppressed because we do reproductive labor: if men could get pregnant, they would be the oppressed sex. Steinem’s concept of a “liberated woman” (who, as she quipped, has sex before marriage and a job after) directly contradicted the the very heart of the radical movement’s argument — that women are oppressed as a class and can’t make themselves free individually. Where did her politics come from? She seemed have one foot in the establishment from the start, dating John F. Kennedy speechwriter Ted Sorensen; then Franklin Thomas, who would soon lead the Ford Foundation; and, in the 1980s, real estate developer Mortimer Zuckerman. Vivian Gornick recalled, “Gloria was uptown; we were downtown. She hung out with Establishment figures; we had only ourselves.” Steinem and the CIA In 1967, the left-wing magazine Ramparts exposed the river of secret CIA money flowing into the National Student Association, the United States’ largest student group. After the revelations, Steinem spoke to the press about her role in recruiting anti-communist students to attend and disrupt the World Youth Festivals, which started in the socialist world and planned for the first time to venture outside the iron curtain in Vienna in 1959 and Helsinki in 1962. She worked full-time as director of the Independent Service for Information on the Vienna Youth Festival, later renamed the Independent Research Service (IRS), a CIA conduit that flooded the festivals with anti-communist and pro-US propaganda. At the Helsinki festival, which drew 18,000 people from 137 countries, the IRS produced a daily newspaper published in three languages, coedited by Steinem and Clay Felker. One of the 1959 publications with her name on it, A Review of Negro Segregation in the United States , claimed that the problem of racial discrimination had essentially been solved in the United States and that leftover problems were due to black people’s psychology. Low voter registration was because “in many areas of the South there exists a profound apathy among Negroes to the this paramount responsibility of good citizenship.” The CIA’s goal had been to make the festivals so fraught — by encouraging violent clashes — that the countries sponsoring them would cancel them. As it turned out, the following two were canceled because the planned hosts, Algeria in 1965 and then Ghana in 1966, experienced coups. In Ghana, the CIA was involved, according to agency officer John Stockwell. In the 1967 interviews, Steinem said the CIA funding was no problem. “Far from being shocked by this involvement I was happy to find some liberals in government in those days who were far-sighted and cared enough to get Americans of all political views to the festival,” she told The New York Times . She also said she was not asked to report on people she met there. Since Steinem wasn’t well-known at the time, it was eight years later that the New York–based feminist group Redstockings discovered the connection, after Steinem had rocketed to the front of the movement. Redstockings published an exposé in 1975, suggesting that the substitution of Ms . and Steinem for the “original, authentic activists that started the movement” looked similar to other CIA operations that “create or support ‘parallel’ organizations which provide an alternative to radicalism.” It also pointed out that a report published by Steinem’s organization on the Vienna festival included short dossiers on dozens of student leaders from around the world — contrary to her claim she never reported on attendees. Steinem at first refused to respond to the charges, but when she did, she again defended her role and that of the CIA at the festivals. However, she did put considerable effort into suppressing the argument made by Redstockings. Random House planned to bring out a mass-market edition of the self-published book Redstockings book Feminist Revolution , which included a chapter on Steinem. Steinem threatened to sue Random House, and the publisher caved and censored the chapter. Steinem’s lawyers also threatened The Village Voice and even sent a threatening letter to every member of the board of the Columbia Tenants Union in New York City when its newspaper, The Heights and Valley News , printed a series on Steinem and the censorship. Women’s Equality and the Neoliberal Turn By the late 1980s, Steinem was famous for Ms . and for being the radical feminist but had not yet written a book laying out her vision of feminism (the anthology Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions in 1983 collected her writing in Ms .and elsewhere). When it finally came, Revolution From Within: A Book of Self-Esteem (1992) affirmed everything about her politics that had dismayed the radicals who started the movement. The book, which received a six-figure advance, continued the women’s magazine line that women needed to make internal changes. “Without self-esteem, the only change is an exchange of masters; with it, there is no need for masters,” she wrote. Of course, we don’t have masters because we need them but because they need us . This basic inversion was symptomatic of her politics. By contrast, women’s liberation feminists argued that women, like other oppressed people, are in constant struggle against our bonds — a concept they called the “Pro-Woman Line” — in fact, we take every bit of space available and find ingenious workarounds even when there is none. It was discrimination, exploitation, punishment, and constant everyday pressure that constrained us. This hard-won analysis was developed through the main program of the movement, consciousness-raising . Ms . watered down this important organizing tool, publishing a guide to consciousness-raising that used the name and the form but missed the substance, reducing it to a therapy group where women blew off steam and got sisterly support. The original idea was to use the data that emerged in testimony to assess women’s true situation, dig at the root cause, and analyze who benefits. The program was inspired by the Southern civil rights movement’s “tell it like it is” public testifying and had parallels in the Chinese Revolution’s “speak bitterness” sessions. It was not intended as a safe space. As corporate attacks in the late 1970s and early ’80s destroyed unions and working-class living conditions and wages plunged for all workers, Friedan and feminist radicals alike argued that advancing women’s equality now required confrontation with corporate power to get guarantees of childcare and health care, paid family leave, and shorter work hours for everyone. Friedan called it the “second stage” of feminism in a book by that name. Redstockings called for the abolition of private health insurance companies and a robust social wage, to give women independence from men and employers. The Ms . wing of the movement fragmented into thousands of nonprofits, competing for grants from rich people by each proposing “winnable” small-bore solutions to the wreckage left by the employer offensive. This blinkered feminist vision was reflected in the Democratic Party establishment. Meanwhile, long hours, low pay, and worsening conditions for raising kids made women vulnerable to a right-wing nostalgia for to the “glorious thirty” postwar years of family-supporting jobs and stay-at-home moms. In recent years, Steinem dropped all pretense of radicalism. She supported Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic primary against Bernie Sanders, and in an interview that year on Real Time With Bill Maher suggested that young women only supported Sanders because “that’s where the boys are; the boys are with Bernie.” She later claimed she misspoke. Media hagiography of Steinem reached a fever pitch in the last decade with a TV dramatization of her life, The Glorias ; a play, Gloria: A Life ; and glowing profiles in the The New York Times , The New Yorker , and elsewhere. This wave of Steinem-mania coincided with a time that young women were questioning the utility of a 1 percent feminism, represented by such figures as Clinton, Madeleine Albright , and Sheryl Sandberg . Had the goal of women’s liberation really been exploitative corporations and a violent US empire run by women? Steinem was again trotted out to steer the discussion into safe channels, but by the time of her appearance with Maher, she was just giving feminists a bad name. Women’s liberation movement pioneers, to a woman, came out of the civil rights movement, the antiwar movement, and the student left. They believed that consistent feminism leads to socialism, and vice versa. Following Beauvoir, they wanted to dig deep and abolish the exploitation of women and the oppression required to maintain it. Starting in the 1960s, they planned and built a successful radical movement that profoundly changed the situation of women in the United States and reverberated worldwide. It’s a crime that their movement was for fifty years personified by someone who never shared its goals.

articles.title: Organizing from the Bottom: IBEW’s Fight for Sanitary Facilities
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: Workers in high-visibility gear gather at a downtown Detroit worksite, with the city skyline visible in the background. By Kevin Szczesny To get clean Porta-johns in our workplace, construction workers at the Marriott site in downtown Detroit marched on the boss. Workers from at least seven unions of the building trades were represented, with zero union staffers or officers present. Many union halls were in support of the action, but the work and the application of leverage were entirely rank-and-file driven. As an active member of IBEW Local 58 (Electrical Workers), I often hear from sympathetic organizers who “can’t imagine how hard it must be” organizing in a largely conservative and obstinate workforce. Our campaign is a contribution to the death of that narrative, and an answer to the universal follow-up question about how these shop floor conversations go in detail. Day One on the job, as I met my 50 or so fellow electricians, I was immediately overwhelmed with warnings that the bathrooms were going to be unsanitary. I knew before the end of my shift that the issue was widely felt, and every electrician already had the same idea: we wanted the cleaning schedule changed from twice a week to three times a week. I had a long conversation with the steward about what efforts were already in progress to correct the issue. The first instinct of a construction worker is to “drag” (quit), drive over to the union hall, and pick up a new job. As expected, there was a steady trickle of drags and conditions on site had not improved. OSHA had been called and walked the job soon after my arrival, only to say that the number of bathrooms was up to their standard. The electrical contractor had been notified, but because the bathrooms were for all of the trades to use, our bosses didn’t feel it was their responsibility to pay for additional cleaning. The local IBEW contract only gestures vaguely to “sanitary facilities,” and protects us explicitly should we leave site to find a “sanitary” facility. This clause was exercised regularly, but no one could say for sure whether the boss was even aware we were leaving. Over time, smaller issues would pop up and get resolved quickly with small actions. Sweeping compound to control toxic dust, unprecedented changes in break time, trades doing the work of other trades out of convenience: these were things that were easily managed by the steward with one or two voices in support. I got involved with a couple pushes and so was asked to fill in for the steward while he was out for a few days. When I walked the job to make sure everyone had my number, more than half the conversations touched on the bathrooms. I then introduced myself to the stewards from the other trades, who all encountered the same comments from their members. The idea was formed to take the issue above our bosses and straight to the general contractor (who hires out each trade and is responsible for the job site at large). A letter was written titled “Unacceptable Bathroom Conditions,” which opened politely and assumed the boss was ignorant of the problem. The letter referenced the impact on our work and a widespread feeling that we were not being treated with respect by the contractor. We suggested that the person responsible for scheduling use our bathrooms for a week, to better assess the need for more cleanings and a wash station. We gave one week for a response. Every worker who was presented with the letter signed immediately, but reactions were mixed. Most people felt like they would just laugh at our demand, but were interested in the idea of swarming the bosses’ trailer at lunch and forcing them to read it in front of us.We fielded many suggestions, from delivering the letter and going home to tipping over Porta-johns on the way to the boss, and we told our coworkers that if our response date came and went without change, we would be coming back around “to have a different conversation.” This demand had to be made collectively and clearly first so that any future action would be naturally tied to the lack of clean facilities, and we had to start our escalation low enough that further demonstrations would be felt. Many of our one-on-one talks were focused on assuring the workers that we would circle back for an escalation if the letter went ignored. “This is only the beginning”, “they probably will ignore this or lie, but we need to show that we’re all on the same page first,” “dragging only leaves behind the people who can’t quit with shitty conditions,” etc. We warned of possible counter-strategies from the boss and stressed the importance of demonstrating solidarity, especially across the trades, above all else. We also left out the officers at the hall and our reps on purpose, though we did inform them. We had a lot of conversations about the power in the hands of the rank-and-file. “Every member is a steward” has become sort of a slogan for us. In the end we had 105 signatures and roughly 35 folks across four trades who gave up their lunch break to deliver the letter. The contractor read that letter, was brought outside to look at us, and immediately conceded to our terms. Maybe they didn’t know how bad the bathrooms were, maybe they didn’t know how widely and deeply felt the issue was on site, or maybe they figured it was fine to ignore. All we know for sure is, when a seemingly small fraction of us came together with the backing of three times as many signatures, it didn’t matter if we had the hall behind us. We are the union, the working people who don’t walk away from a job which doesn’t satisfy us, and our demands have been met. Kevin is a trade unionist and has been a member of the IBEW for two years and DSA member for five. Organizing from the Bottom: IBEW’s Fight for Sanitary Facilities was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Healthy food is still out of reach for students and young people
articles.author: Peoples Health Dispatch
articles.content: Students in secondary schools across England remain reliant on unhealthy food amid ongoing commercialization, weak accountability, and inaccessible prices. A recent report by the network Bite Back examines how these intersecting factors are affecting children’s nutrition, calling on the government to revise existing standards and ensure students can access real, nutritious food. Read more: Ultra-processed food dominates child nutrition in the UK The report found that a significant number of secondary school students still opt for “grab-and-go” items over full school meals. These predominantly carbohydrate-based options, such as pastries and chips, mostly fall short of existing nutritional standards. But while the food industry often argues that students reach for these items based on individual preference, the report and students themselves warn that choice is largely driven by convenience and price. Grab-and-go items are consistently the least expensive option available in schools. The report found that in some institutions, the cheapest main meal can cost nearly five times as much as the cheapest grab-and-go item. This pricing structure makes processed snacks more accessible to students on free school meals, implying a disproportionate health – and thus education – impact on children from working-class families. According to the report, 56% of students on free school meals relied on grab-and-go options for lunch at least 3–4 times per week, compared to 36% of students not involved in the program. This disparity should not be attributed to different food preferences, the report insists. “Only one in three survey respondents felt grab-and-go leaves them with enough energy to concentrate in lessons, and multiple focus group participants reported feeling hunger, fatigue and loss of focus later in the day,” Bite Back wrote. Read more: Industry remains biggest barrier to tackling ultra-processed food harm The prominence of unhealthy options is the result of several factors: rising food costs, policy choices that have failed to shield the education sector, and a food system driven largely by profit-seeking – with secondary school students identified as a promising commercial market and referred to as “customers.” “Grab-and-go food and drinks are attractive to suppliers and caterers because they deliver higher profit margins and make up a large share of total sales,” the report notes. “Healthy foods tend to be expensive to produce but high-calorie, nutrient-poor snacks, often sold two or three times across a school day, are cheaper and sell well.” Or, as one interviewee summarized: “The commercial pressures aren’t to serve wonderfully fresh, healthy food. It’s to serve junk because there’s money in it.” With the government preparing to expand free school meals , campaigners are calling for clearer accountability guidelines and measures to help schools shape food programs around health and nutrition recommendations. Bite Back has also urged action to curb commercial incentives favoring unhealthy options, investment in canteen infrastructure, and adequate funding for free school meals. People’s Health Dispatch is a fortnightly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . For more articles and to subscribe to People’s Health Dispatch, click here .

articles.title: ‘You won, Mr. President’: Press freedom under attack in Ecuador
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: A few days ago, one of Ecuador’s most widely followed journalists, Gisella Bayona, announced that she would quit journalism due to pressure from the administration, led by right-wing President Daniel Noboa. “In recent hours, a pro-government media outlet has published serious accusations against me and my husband, attempting to link my questions about the lack of medicines in hospitals to personal interests.” Bayona was referring to the investigations she had conducted regarding the severe and chronic shortage of medicines and medical supplies in the public health system that has plagued the country for several years. Noboa has repeatedly promised to resolve this problem, but so far there has been no solution, while the number of deaths due to a lack of public health care continues to rise. With regard to patients with kidney problems alone, some media outlets have reported that more than 4,000 people have died due to a lack of care , a figure that has sparked significant controversy in Ecuador. In this regard, on August 28, President Noboa said on a local radio station that he found it outrageous that a journalist (whose name he did not mention) would speak on this issue when her husband had financial interests in the medicine supply business. He also accused this journalist’s husband of having ties to former Vice President Jorge Glas, who is currently in prison. Bayona has categorically denied the accusations and stated that the media outlet attacking her allegedly manipulated information to make her look bad. In light of this, Bayona announced her retirement from journalism: “I will not allow my family to be attacked without any basis simply because of my journalistic inquiries … Mr. President, you won. You have the power and the means to impose any narrative. I can withstand attacks against me, but I cannot put my family at risk.” In this regard, sociologist Fernando Muñoz wrote : “What kind of world do we live in where the act of criticism ends up leading to the conclusion that remaining silent seems like a reasonable alternative? In that sense, the phrase ‘you won’ doesn’t mean that Daniel Noboa defeated Bayona in the arena of ideas through better arguments, but rather expresses the enormous asymmetry that exists between a journalist who asks questions and a political power that has at its disposal institutions, public resources, communication channels, and a digital machine capable of amplifying narratives to its advantage.” Furthermore, Muño said : “‘Mr. President, you won,’ said Gissela Bayona before leaving journalism. That statement should be unbearable for any government that still claims to be democratic – not because the president has to share a journalist’s opinions or because the media should be exempt from criticism, but because in a democracy, the victory of those in power can never consist of getting those who hold them accountable to stop doing so out of fear.” Other cases of alleged pressure against journalists Bayona’s announcement has sparked widespread criticism of the government, which is accused of repressing several journalists critical of the Noboa administration. But it has also drawn applause from government supporters, who argue that Bayona clearly has a conflict of interest when reporting on the issue. However, Bayona’s case is not the only one that has drawn criticism from journalists in Ecuador, including those from right-wing media outlets. While the censorship of left-wing journalism has become common (however dishonorable), right-wing journalism in Ecuador has, with a few exceptions, enjoyed a relatively broad scope for criticism when it has exercised that right. But the cases of Bayona and other right-wing journalists who have had to give up journalism or have been fired from their media outlets due to alleged pressure from those in power have sparked a massive wave of criticism against the government for undermining freedom of expression. In 2024, Cuban journalist Alondra Santiago had her visa revoked for allegedly committing acts against state security – a charge the journalist, who is close to the Correa movement, categorically denied. Something similar happened to the Spanish-Chilean journalist Lautaro Bernat, who was deported from Ecuador while covering the protests against the Noboa administration in 2025. According to the government, the decision was based on a confidential report citing national security concerns. During the demonstrations, the NGO Fundamedios reported 31 attacks against the press. Likewise, there have been reports of alleged pressure on private media outlets to dismiss journalists. The most emblematic case is that of Roberto Aguilar , a journalist with clear right-wing leanings and one of the country’s most celebrated editorialists, who in recent months has publicly criticized the government’s handling of the situation. According to the lawyer for the newspaper Expreso , the Noboa administration reportedly requested that the company managing the publication dismiss Aguilar. Following this, the Superintendency of Companies reportedly intervened in the company to pressure it into changing its editorial line. Ultimately, Aguilar was dismissed from the newspaper Expreso on August 12, 2026. Another high-profile case involved Hernán Higuera , a journalist with the country’s largest television network, Ecuavisa , who produced a series of investigative reports on the so-called Progen Case, which refers to a series of government purchases of electric generators during the Noboa administration to alleviate the severe energy crisis facing the country, and in which the prosecutor’s office alleges that the country suffered losses of nearly $100 million as a result of corruption. After several reports, Higuera announced on television that he would stop reporting on this matter due to the pressure he was receiving. Specifically, Higuera stated that following the reports, his wife, a public official, was dismissed from her position, and his son lost his position at the medical residency program, among other consequences. These are some of the cases that have provoked heavy criticisms of the Noboa administration, including from international organizations. The Inter-American Press Association (SIP) stated in its Chapultepec Index that Ecuador is experiencing its worst period for press freedom since 2020, with its score dropping from 46.03 to 38.42 out of 100 points, and the country being categorized as one with “High Restrictions” on press freedom.
